idea: Halftone close-up of a compositor's hand holding a composing stick full of metal sorts, letters reading mirror-reversed, captioned 'Every word, backwards first.' For people who love the craft and the patient mental flip every hand typesetter did all day.

Archive photo of a Linotype operator at the huge clattering keyboard-and-magazine machine, captioned 'A line o' type, cast in hot lead.' The machine got its name from casting a whole line as one metal slug. A tribute to the industrial monster behind every newspaper for about 80 years.

The 1940 photograph of the bombed library at Holland House, London: the roof gone, rubble on the floor, and men calmly browsing the shelves that are still standing. Captioned 'Still browsing.' It's quiet defiance for anyone who believes reading is worth doing even in the ruins.

WPA photo of a Kentucky Pack Horse Library carrier on horseback, saddlebags full of books, heading up a mountain trail, captioned 'The library came to you. 1935–1943.' A true New Deal story of women who rode remote routes so isolated families could read.

Archive photo of an 1870s Sholes and Glidden typewriter, captioned 'QWERTY. Designed in the 1870s. Still typing.' A dry nod to the 150-year-old layout under every keyboard, including the one the wearer is using right now.

Old museum photograph of the Rosetta Stone, captioned 'Same decree. Three scripts.' (hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek). For translators, linguists and anyone who knows that one stone made it possible to read a whole civilization again.

A Lewis Hine photograph of a young newsboy calling out headlines with a bundle of papers under his arm, captioned with one word: 'EXTRA.' Strong documentary imagery, and a quiet comment on what it took to get the news out.

Library photo of a wall of wooden card-catalog drawers stretching out of frame, captioned 'Search engine, oak, c. 1900.' A wink for librarians and information nerds who know that indexing the world began long before the internet.

Photograph of an open Gutenberg Bible spread showing its two dense blackletter columns, captioned '42 lines.' Book people will know it's the '42-line Bible,' the book that started printing with movable type in Europe. Everyone else just sees a beautiful page.

Archive photo of a blind reader's fingertips moving across a page of embossed braille, captioned 'Six dots. Invented by Louis Braille at 15.' A lovely image of reading by touch, with a fact that makes people stop.

Photo of a 19th-century Morse telegraph key, captioned 'What hath God wrought' and '1844'. That was the first official message Samuel Morse sent from Washington to Baltimore. It's the first text message, and a question that still fits every new medium.

Archive photo of a bookbinder's hands sewing folded signatures on a sewing frame, captioned 'Hand-sewn. Built to outlast the format wars.' A craft-pride shirt for people who keep paper books and know why bindings last.

Photograph of the 1623 First Folio open at its title page with the Droeshout portrait, captioned '18 plays that exist because of this book.' Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night were first printed there. It's a real argument for publishing as preservation.

The US National Archives photograph of the Berlin book burning of 10 May 1933, captioned with Heinrich Heine's line from 1821: 'Where they burn books, they will in the end burn people too.' A serious, beautiful, uncompromising shirt for readers who see book bans as an early warning.

The archive portrait of OED editor James Murray in his 'Scriptorium' shed, surrounded by pigeonholes of quotation slips, captioned 'He made it to T.' He died in 1915 while working on T, and the dictionary was finished in 1928. Dark humour about a life's work too big for one life.

NASA photograph of the Voyager Golden Record, captioned 'Hello, in 55 languages. Mailed 1977. Still in transit.' It's language as humanity's message in a bottle, and the record is still travelling out of the solar system.

Early-20th-century photo of one marble lion outside the New York Public Library, captioned 'Patience and Fortitude.' Mayor La Guardia named the pair in the 1930s for the qualities New Yorkers needed. It's a motto for readers and anyone in a long project.

The c. 1847 daguerreotype of the teenage Emily Dickinson, captioned 'About 1,800 poems. About 10 published while she lived.' A shirt for writers that says the work counts whether or not anyone notices it yet.

Archive portrait of L. L. Zamenhof, captioned 'Esperanto: one who hopes.' He published his international language in 1887 under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, and the name stuck to the language. An idealistic, nerdy shirt about a language invented to bring people together.

US Marine Corps WWII photograph of Navajo Code Talkers at a field radio, captioned 'The code was never broken.' The code was built on the Navajo language, which had little written form at the time. It honours a language that the US government had tried to suppress in schools.
